To holster something means to put a weapon — almost always a handgun — back into its holster after you have taken it out.

A holster is the snug pouch or case (usually made of leather or tough plastic) that holds a handgun. It is typically attached to a belt around the waist, strapped to the thigh, or worn under the arm. When you holster a gun, you are sliding it safely back into that holder and securing it there.

Think of it this way: a sword goes into a scabbard, an arrow goes into a quiver, and a gun goes into a holster. The verb follows the same logic — to holster is to put the gun back in its home.

This is the most important thing to lock into your memory:

Holster always means putting the weapon away, never taking it out.

Taking a gun out of a holster is called drawing (as in, "he drew his weapon"). Putting it back is holstering.

So:

  • A detective pulls out her gun to face a suspect → she draws her weapon.
  • The situation is resolved and she puts it away → she holsters her weapon.
Who Uses This Word, and When

You will most commonly encounter "holster" as a verb in these real-world contexts:

  • Law enforcement: Police officers are trained on exactly when to draw and when to holster. "The officer holstered his gun once the scene was secure."
  • Military: Soldiers and armed personnel holster their sidearms when they are not in immediate use.
  • Security guards: Armed guards holster their weapons routinely throughout a shift.
  • Shooting ranges: Instructors give commands like "holster your firearm" to signal the end of a round of shooting.
  • Fiction: Books, films, and TV shows use it constantly. A cowboy in a Western holsters his revolver after a showdown. A spy holsters her pistol after neutralizing a threat.
A Crucial Detail — What It Implies

When someone holsters a weapon, it carries a specific emotional and situational weight. It signals:

  • The danger has passed. You only safely put a gun away when you no longer need it ready.
  • Control and discipline. Knowing when to holster is just as important as knowing when to draw. A well-trained officer holsters promptly once a threat is over — it is a sign of professionalism, not carelessness.
  • A return to a neutral, safe state. The weapon is accessible, but no longer active or pointed at anything.

While less common than "draw," the word unholster exists and is used. It simply means to take a weapon out of its holster.

  • "He unholstered his weapon when he heard the noise." (= He took his gun out.)
  • "She holstered her weapon after the arrest." (= She put her gun away.)

Language loves to borrow from the physical world, and "holster" is no exception. In informal, figurative speech, people sometimes use "holster" to mean to put something away, hold something back, or stop using/wielding something — even when no gun is involved.

Examples:

  • "Holster the attitude." → Put your aggression away; calm down.
  • "Holster that sarcasm for a moment." → Stop being sarcastic right now.
  • "You can holster the legal threats — we'll sort this out." → You don't need to threaten legal action; let's talk.

In each case, the core idea is the same: stop brandishing this thing and put it away. The "thing" just doesn't have to be a gun.

What it meansTo place a gun (or figuratively, anything powerful) back into its holster/away from active use
DirectionAlways away / in — never taking out
OppositeTo draw (or to unholster)
ContextPolice, military, security, Western/action fiction; informally, any act of putting something aggressive away

The single clearest sentence you can carry with you: To holster is to put a weapon safely away after use. Everything else — the figurative uses, the emotional implications, the professional context — flows naturally from that core idea.
